newsitem.title: GERMANY: Strict compliance vital for stable euro - Duisenberg.
newsitem.headline: Strict compliance vital for stable euro - Duisenberg.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said on Wednesday he supported a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty to govern which countries join Europe's single currency project in 1999.

Duisenberg, who takes over this summer as chief of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) and is tipped to take over a post-EMU European Central Bank, also said sustained fulfilment of treaty criteria was vital to ensure a stable euro currency.

"Considering the need to create a stable monetary union I would draw your attention to the significance of a strict interpretation of the convergence criteria," he said in a speech given to a forum on European monetary union (EMU).
Duisenberg said that any delay to EMU's 1999 start if countries missed the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria this year could be risky. "I fear that a delay would lead to a permanent delay."

The Maastricht treaty does not foresee a postponement of the launch of the single euro currency, he said. Although some legal experts say such a delay was possible, he considered that to be "very dangerous."
"I believe it would then be necessary to renegotiate the treaty and for it to be ratified by all 15 parliaments (in the European Union)," Duisenberg said.

Asked which of the two targets was the most important -- close convergence to the Maastricht Treaty or the 1999 start date -- Duisenberg said: "I think that if we are very close to the criteria, that is more important."
"If we are far away it would be impossible to hold to the date. We are working in Europe to come closer to the criteria."
Duisenberg is a leading candidate to take over at the ECB, which he said must be independent to ensure a strong euro.

In the Maastricht treaty, he noted, "it is forbidden to give orders to the ECB or to try to influence its directors. That does not, by the way, prevent central bank directors exchanging views with their finance ministers."
The Dutch central bank chief also said the so-called stability pact, a mechanism to enforce budgetary discipline, offered guarantees for sound state finances within EMU.
"A key element of this pact is that countries both within and outside EMU must commit to achieving a budget position which is almost in balance or even in surplus," he said.

"A budget which on average is close to balance creates room to cope with cyclical and non-cyclical shocks, without the deficit overstepping the limit of three percent of GDP defined in the the treaty."
"The pact is thus not rigid, but creates room for manoeuvre within the limits defined by the Maastricht treaty," he said.
However, Duisenberg said that "there would be no point" in starting monetary union without Germany.

Germany has said that its national debt will rise this year above 60 percent of GDP and Finance Minister Theo Waigel is struggling to reduce the budget deficit below three percent of GDP while handicapped by record post-war unemployment.
Bonn's efforts to meet the Maastricht fiscal criteria illustrated that European states above all are having problems meeting the budget criteria, Duisenberg said.
But, if countries manage to control borrowing, they can create a virtuous cycle which reduces interests, cuts debt costs, boosts investor confidence and leads to lower inflation.
"As I said, countries can only join the third stage who fit into a stable monetary union. Countries prove that with achievements which demonstrate lasting convergence," he said.
